title: Lesson 2 - Scenario Trade-offs for Agentforce Sales Solution Design
description: Given business requirements, metrics, key performance indicators, or business challenges, determine the optimal solution in Agentforce Sales.

questions.question: A firm wants an agent to draft and send follow-up emails autonomously, but legal requires that no discounting language ever reaches a customer. Which is the strongest design?
options: Constrain the topic instructions and route discount-related replies to a human approval action
Give the agent a longer instruction and rely on the model to comply
Disable the Einstein Trust Layer so the agent has fewer restrictions
Turn off data masking so the agent can see more fields
questions.explanation: Narrow topic instructions plus an approval action for the risky path is the bounded design, and disabling the Trust Layer or masking would weaken protections rather than solve the legal requirement.

questions.question: A 300-rep org has clean CRM data and a fully fixed, auditable approval process with no natural-language input. What should you recommend instead of an autonomous agent?
options: An Agentforce agent with five custom topics
Einstein Activity Capture for the reps
A Flow-based approval because the process is deterministic
questions.explanation: A fixed, auditable process with no conversational input is exactly what Flow is built for, while an agent adds nondeterminism and consumption cost the scenario does not need.

questions.question: Before going live with an Agentforce sales agent, the team must protect customer data sent to the model. Which control applies?
options: Turn off field history tracking on the objects
Enable Salesforce Meetings for the pilot group
The Einstein Trust Layer with data masking and zero data retention
Create a scheduled report subscription for the transcripts
questions.explanation: The Trust Layer sits inline between the agent and the model and provides masking and zero data retention, while none of the other options touch data sent to the LLM.
